title: Cyberattack Disrupts Hundreds of French Supermarkets
paragraphs: A massive cyberattack disrupted hundreds of French supermarkets during the night of October 11 into October 12, as hackers manipulated refrigeration systems, causing food spoilage and fires.

About 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected, according to French Finance Minister Roland Lescure. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies, but called the attack "a wake-up call for everyone."

French supermarket group Groupement Mousquetaires said 300 of its Intermarché and Netto stores were affected, while grocery chain Cooperative U reported 80 stores hit. Carrefour and Monoprix supermarkets were also targeted.
The Paris prosecutor's office said that its cybercrime unit opened an investigation into the attack, including the extent of damage from spoiled food and reported fires.
French broadcaster BFM-TV reported that hackers manipulated refrigeration systems by forcing them into continuous defrost cycles and setting temperatures to as high as 50 degrees Celsius.
The affected remote-control systems, used to monitor and adjust refrigeration equipment from a distance, were made by Danish company Danfoss and US-based Copeland.

Danfoss said most of the affected equipment consisted of older products that no longer received software or security updates. It also said customers had long been advised to keep supported systems updated and behind firewalls.

An August report by US cybersecurity company Claroty identified vulnerabilities in Danfoss and Copeland systems used to manage refrigeration equipment in supermarkets, warehouses and other facilities.
For example, Claroty said some controllers using the Danfoss system were accessible directly from the public internet. But Claroty also said both companies had since addressed the vulnerabilities.
Cybersecurity expert Christopher Whyte of Virginia Commonwealth University said attacks on systems controlling physical infrastructure are not new, with water and power systems targeted for years.
What made the French attack unusual, he said, was its scale, and the fact that there appeared to be no ransom demand or data theft.
It was unclear whether the French cyberattack involved AI.

Varun Chandrasekaran, an engineering professor at the University of Illinois, said advances in AI have contributed to an increase in cybersecurity incidents, and are expected to make such attacks more common.
But he said AI could also help prevent future hacks.
